young.html: Werner Heisenberg was a German physicist who, at just 23, worked out a new way to describe atoms. Two years later he found one of the most famous rules in science: the uncertainty principle.

Here is the idea. To see where something is, you have to bounce light off it. For a baseball that is no problem. But an electron is so tiny that the light itself gives it a kick. The more exactly you find where it is, the less you can know about how fast it is moving, and the other way around. It is like a seesaw: push one end down and the other goes up.
Heisenberg came to think this is not just a problem with our tools. It is how nature is. Tiny things like electrons don’t have an exact place and an exact speed at the same moment.

young.html: The blurry photo game. Ask someone to roll a ball across the floor while you take a photo. With a very fast shutter, the ball looks sharp: you know where it is, but the photo can’t show which way or how fast it was going. With a slow shutter, the ball becomes a streak: you can see its motion, but not exactly where it was. This is only a picture of the idea (for a ball, both can be known well), but it shows the kind of trade-off Heisenberg found for atoms.

full.html: Werner Heisenberg (1901–1976) studied with Arnold Sommerfeld in Munich and worked with Max Born in Göttingen and Niels Bohr in Copenhagen. In June 1925, on the island of Helgoland where he had gone to recover from hay fever, he found the first form of quantum mechanics (matrix mechanics). In 1927 he stated the uncertainty principle. He received the Nobel Prize for 1932.

During the Second World War he was a leading scientist in Germany’s nuclear research program. What he intended, and why the program never came close to a bomb, has been debated by historians ever since. After the war he helped rebuild German science.

Physics and Philosophy: The Revolution in Modern Science (1958) grew from his Gifford Lectures at the University of St Andrews, Scotland, in the winter of 1955–56. It tells the history of quantum theory, sets out the Copenhagen interpretation, and compares it with Greek philosophy, Descartes, Kant and modern ideas about language.
This book was first published in 1958, so it is still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of it. Everything here is our own summary.

In quantum mechanics a particle is described by a wave. A wave squeezed into a small region of space must be built of many wavelengths, and a particle’s wavelength fixes its momentum. So a narrow spread in position $\Delta x$ forces a wide spread in momentum $\Delta p$:

$\Delta x \, \Delta p \ \ge\ \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$, where $\hbar = h/2\pi \approx 1.055 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. Momentum is mass times velocity, so for a particle of mass $m$, $\Delta v \ge \hbar / (2 m \Delta x)$.

full.html: Heisenberg first explained it with a thought experiment, a microscope for seeing an electron. To see it sharply you need light of short wavelength, but short-wavelength light carries a big, unpredictable kick, so the better you see where the electron is, the more you disturb its motion. Bohr pointed out that the microscope story is only part of it: the limit comes from the wave description itself, not just from clumsy measuring. Heisenberg accepted this.

full.title: An electron in an atom
full.q: An electron (mass $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg) is confined to a region about the size of an atom, $\Delta x = 1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. What is the least spread in its velocity?
full.a: About 580 km/s: huge. An electron in an atom can’t sit still.

full.title: A baseball
full.q: A baseball (0.145 kg) is located to within 1 micrometer ($10^{-6}$ m). What is the least spread in its velocity?
full.a: About $4 \times 10^{-28}$ m/s: far too small ever to notice. That is why everyday objects seem to have exact places and speeds.

items: The Copenhagen interpretation. We must describe experiments in the concepts of classical physics (position, momentum, wave, particle), though they apply to atoms only in limited, complementary ways. The wave function gives probabilities; the act of observation turns a range of possibilities into one fact.
Potentiality. Heisenberg suggests that the quantum wave is like Aristotle’s potentia: a tendency toward events, something between an idea and a fact.

Greek roots. He finds Heraclitus, who made fire (change) the basic stuff of the world, close to modern physics, where energy turns into particles and back. And he thinks the smallest particles are less like Democritus’ tiny solid atoms than like the mathematical forms of Plato’s Timaeus.
Language. Ordinary words were made for everyday things; when we use them about atoms we must know their limits.

full.html: Thinking the uncertainty principle means scientists are careless, or that “anything goes.” It is an exact, tested law, and it lets physicists make very precise predictions, for example of atomic spectra and of how transistors work.

The uncertainty principle has passed every test and is part of every physics course. The book is widely read as a thoughtful scientist’s view of his own revolution. Its interpretation is another matter. Einstein, de Broglie, David Bohm and others proposed alternatives, which Heisenberg discusses and rejects in one chapter; later the many-worlds view and others joined the list. Physicists still disagree about what, if anything, the wave function describes, though they agree on the predictions. Historians, for their part, continue to weigh Heisenberg’s wartime role.

items: Aristotle’s Physics, earlier on this ladder, distinguished the potential from the actual; Heisenberg borrows the distinction for the quantum wave.
Plato’s Timaeus built the elements from mathematical shapes. Heisenberg thought modern particle physics was closer to Plato than to the atomists.
Lucretius and the atomists pictured hard, unchanging atoms. Heisenberg’s particles can be created and destroyed.
Bohr, two rungs back, gave the philosophy of complementarity that Heisenberg follows; Einstein remained its great critic.
Does a particle have an exact position before anyone measures it?
Can old philosophers help us understand new physics, or are the resemblances only on the surface?
Are there limits to what can ever be known, and is it good to know where they are?

questions: Can you think of a situation where knowing one thing very exactly makes it harder to know another?
Why is it that the uncertainty principle matters for electrons but not for baseballs?
Heisenberg found old Greek ideas in new physics. Why might very old questions still matter to scientists?
Historians disagree about Heisenberg’s choices in the war. How should we judge people who lived through hard times?
Is it unsettling or exciting that nature has built-in limits to what we can know?
